title: SAL2
lead: TryHackMe's advanced SOC cert, built with NCC Group. Over 72 hours you work 12 multi-stage incidents across three simulated SOC shifts, then make the calls and write the reports a Tier 2 analyst would. It proves you can run an investigation end to end, not just triage alerts.
objSub: Seven areas from TryHackMe's SAL2 exam overview. Tick objectives as you study them; progress saves on this device.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan splits about 120 hours across the seven areas, then saves the last stretch for full scenario practice with written reports.
pbqSub: Practice in the style of the exam: half technical investigation, half decisions and reporting.

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: Each scenario takes about 45 minutes to 2 hours. Scoring is two equal halves: technical (about 7 questions per scenario tracing the attack chain and IOCs) and non-technical (a decision exercise plus an AI-graded incident summary). Unproctored, results are instant, and one free retake is included. SAL1 isn't required, but TryHackMe recommends it first.
cur.onote: Areas from TryHackMe's SAL2 exam overview; the lines under each come from TryHackMe's list of domains covered. TryHackMe publishes no weights for these areas, so the bars show an even split.

extras.title: A Tier 2 incident summary
rows: One or two sentences a leader can read: what happened, to what, and how bad.
First sign, initial access, spread, detection and containment, in order.
Hosts, accounts, data and systems involved, and what was ruled out.
IPs, domains, hashes, accounts and the ATT&CK techniques seen.
What was contained, reset, blocked or collected.
Remaining steps, owners and the new detections to add.

extras.title: Where to look
rows: Success and failure, with logon type and source.
What ran, its parent, and its command line.
Spikes for service accounts can mean Kerberoasting.
Who changed what in the account, and from where.
Risky sign-ins, impossible travel, MFA results.

method: Make sure SAL1-level triage is solid. SAL2 assumes you can already work a queue.
Work TryHackMe's SOC Level 2 path, plus its threat hunting and DFIR modules.
After every lab, write a short incident summary. Reporting is half the score.
Practice SIEM queries in Splunk and Elastic until pivoting from an alert is quick.
Do a few long scenarios back to back, timed, to practice working across 72 hours.
tips: Twelve scenarios at up to 2 hours each, plus sleep. Schedule your shifts like a real SOC.
Keep a timeline and IOC list for each scenario. It feeds the questions and the report.
The decision exercise rewards the reason as much as the choice: impact, evidence, SLA.
Executives get impact and actions; DFIR gets evidence and timeline.

quiz.q: Order matters in a report. Which sequence of attacker steps is in the right kill-chain order?
o: Phishing email, macro runs, scheduled task added, credentials dumped, RDP to a file server
Right. Initial access, execution, persistence, credential access, then lateral movement.
RDP to a file server, phishing email, credentials dumped, macro runs
Lateral movement can't come before initial access.
Credentials dumped, phishing email, macro runs, scheduled task added
Dumping credentials needs a foothold first.
Scheduled task added, phishing email, RDP, macro runs
Persistence comes after the attacker gets in.

quiz.q: A user forwarded a phishing email. What should you check FIRST to scope the incident?
o: Who else received it and who clicked or opened the attachment
Right. One report usually means many recipients. Scope before you close it.
Whether the sender's company has a good website
Irrelevant; sender domains are easily spoofed or look-alikes.
The user's job title
It doesn't tell you how far the email spread.
The email's font
Not useful evidence.

quiz.q: An alert fires for a hash your threat intel platform scores as known ransomware, seen on one laptop. The EDR shows it was quarantined before running. What's the BEST severity call?
o: Medium: confirmed malicious but blocked; verify containment and how it arrived
Right. The threat is real but didn't execute. Confirm that, then find the delivery path.
Critical: declare a ransomware incident across the enterprise
Nothing ran and only one host saw it. That overreacts.
Low: close it because the EDR handled it
Still find out how it got there, or it will come back.
Informational: ignore threat intel matches
A known-ransomware match always deserves a look.

quiz.q: Which enrichment adds the MOST context to a suspicious outbound IP?
o: Reputation, hosting provider, first-seen date and other hosts that contacted it
Right. That tells you if it's known-bad, new and how widely it's reached.
The IP's binary form
That's just a number format.
The time zone of the analyst
Unrelated.
Whether the IP is even or odd
Meaningless.

quiz.q: You found an attacker running encoded PowerShell launched by Word. What's the BEST way to make sure it's caught next time?
o: Write a Sigma rule for powershell.exe with an encoded command whose parent is winword.exe
Right. Sigma turns the behavior into a portable detection for your SIEM.
Block the attacker's IP only
IPs change. The behavior is the better signal.
Uninstall PowerShell everywhere
Admins and tools need it; detection is the better answer.
Add the user to a watch list
It's the behavior, not the user, that needs a rule.

quiz.q: In the SIEM, an alert shows a strange process on host WS-22. What's a good next pivot?
o: Look at its process tree, user, network connections and the same hash on other hosts
Right. Pivoting from one alert to its context and spread is core Tier 2 work.
Close it because only one host is affected
You don't know that until you check the hash elsewhere.
Reimage WS-22 immediately without looking
You'd destroy evidence before you understand the incident.
Email the user and wait for an answer
Investigate the telemetry first.

quiz.q: A service account requests Kerberos service tickets (event 4769) for 60 different services in a minute, using RC4 encryption. What does this suggest?
o: Kerberoasting
Right. Requesting many service tickets, often with RC4, lets an attacker crack service account passwords offline.
A normal backup job
Backups don't request tickets for dozens of different services at once.
A DNS outage
DNS problems don't create a burst of Kerberos ticket requests.
A password spray
Spraying shows as failed logons for many accounts.

quiz.q: Entra ID shows a user signing in from Norfolk, then from another continent 20 minutes later, both successful. What's the FIRST check?
o: Whether it's impossible travel from a stolen session or token, versus a VPN or proxy
Right. Rule out known VPN egress, then treat it as a likely account compromise.
Whether the user likes to travel
No one travels between continents in 20 minutes.
Whether the Wi-Fi was slow
Unrelated.
Whether the license is active
That doesn't explain the sign-in.

quiz.q: A web server log shows GET /uploads/img.php?cmd=whoami returning 200. What is MOST likely?
o: A web shell was uploaded and is being used to run commands
Right. A PHP file in an upload folder taking a cmd parameter is a classic web shell.
A normal image request
Images aren't PHP files that take commands.
A search engine crawler
Crawlers don't send cmd=whoami.
A failed login
Nothing here is a login.

quiz.q: Two cases are open: a medium-severity phishing click with a 4-hour SLA (3.5 hours used) and a low-severity policy alert with a 24-hour SLA (1 hour used). Which do you work first?
o: The phishing click: higher severity and about to breach its SLA
Right. Severity and SLA both point to the phishing case.
The policy alert, because it's easier
Easy doesn't beat severity and an expiring SLA.
Whichever came in first
Arrival order isn't how a SOC prioritizes.
Neither until the next shift
Waiting breaches the SLA.

quiz.q: A domain admin account is being used from a workstation that never uses admin rights, and it's creating new accounts right now. What's the BEST immediate response?
o: Contain: disable or reset the account and isolate the workstation, then escalate
Right. An active compromise of a privileged account needs containment first.
Watch for another day to gather more evidence
An attacker with domain admin can do enormous damage in a day.
Send a reminder about password policy
Far too slow for an active attack.
Close it as an admin doing their job
New accounts from an unusual workstation is not normal admin work.

quiz.q: Which line belongs in the EXECUTIVE summary rather than the technical report?
o: Payroll data on one server may have been viewed; the server was isolated within 2 hours
Right. Impact and action in plain words is what leaders need.
Process 4412 spawned cmd.exe /c whoami from w3wp.exe
That's technical detail for the DFIR team.
SHA-256 of the dropped binary
An IOC for the technical report.
The Splunk query used to find it
Useful to analysts, not executives.

quiz.q: What makes an incident summary MOST useful for a DFIR handoff?
o: A clear timeline, affected hosts and accounts, IOCs and actions already taken
Right. The next team can pick up without redoing your work.
A long description of every tool you tried
Notes on failed attempts don't help the handoff.
Only the final verdict
Without evidence and scope, DFIR has to start over.
Screenshots with no captions
Uncaptioned images are hard to use.

pbqs.title: Prioritize and respond
pbqs.scenario: Start of shift: five open cases. Pick each one's priority and the immediate action. Some options aren't used.

rows.req: Ransomware note found on a file server; encryption still running
rows.why: Active, spreading damage: contain immediately and escalate.

rows.req: One user clicked a phishing link; no credential entry seen yet
rows.why: Possible compromise: check sign-ins and the endpoint before deciding.

rows.req: Alert fires daily on the backup server's known nightly job
rows.why: A known-good pattern causing noise: tune the rule.

rows.req: Impossible-travel sign-in for an admin, followed by an MFA change
rows.why: Admin account takeover signs: contain the account and escalate.

rows.req: Port scan from the approved vulnerability scanner during its window
rows.why: Authorized and expected: close as benign.

keep.text: SAL2 is valid for 3 years, with a QR-verifiable certificate. Renew by passing the exam again.
SAL2 isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix (V3.0). On its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: For Cyber Defense Analyst (511) and Incident Responder (531), CySA+ and CCNA Cybersecurity are listed.
